summary: A freeCodeCamp forum thread in which Mei asks why an ES6 arrow-function version of a .map() call that returns an object literal works, while the ES5 function version gives a syntax error. Responders explain that the ES5 function body lacks a return statement and the object needs braces; Mei posts a working version with return and parentheses, and ilenia notes that arrow functions allow an implicit return when the body is a single expression.
one_line: Forum thread explaining why an ES5 .map() callback returning an object literal fails while the ES6 arrow version works.
key_facts: Mei is working through the JavaScript course on freeCodeCamp in the section 'Using .map() to extract data from an array'.
Mei's ES6 code was var rating = watchList.map(e => ({ title: e.Title, rating: e.imdbRating })), which works.
Mei's ES5 version used watchList.map(function(e){ title: e.Title, rating: e.imdbRating }) and produced a syntax error.
ArielLeslie replied on October 16, 2019 that the ES5 function doesn't return anything and is missing the braces around the object.
Mei's working ES5 solution was watchList.map(function(e){ return ({title: e.Title, rating: e.imdbRating}) }), posted October 16, 2019.
Onosgb advised using the return keyword before the object literal on October 16, 2019.
ilenia replied on October 17, 2019 that with arrow syntax, if the function body is just a return statement, an implicit return can be used.
ilenia gave the example that x => { return x/2 } is the same as x => x/2.
